subtype: Approach: revise after rejection through feedback [Revision]
passage:
Chinmay: Ninth rejection this month 😔
Tushar: Ouch. Did any of them say why?
Chinmay: Not one. So today I emailed two recruiters and asked for a single honest line on what to fix.
Tushar: And?
Chinmay: One replied within hours! It said my portfolio has nice screens but no business context. No numbers, no problem statement.
Tushar: So what's the plan?
Chinmay: Rebuilding the first project from scratch. Who the users were, what was going wrong for them, what changed after. Probably takes the whole week.
Tushar: Better than sending the same file to ten more places.
Chinmay: Yeah. Those rejections weren't saying I'm bad. They were pointing at what's missing 🙂

qa.q: What did the recruiter say was missing from Chinmay's portfolio?
qa.a: The portfolio had no business context: no numbers and no problem statement.

qa.q: How does Chinmay feel about the rejections by the end of the chat?
qa.a: Chinmay feels steadier and a little hopeful, since the rejections are now read as pointers to what is missing rather than a sign of being bad.

qa.q: What could Chinmay add to this approach, and why?
qa.a: Chinmay could ask a working professional to read the rebuilt portfolio before sending it out, because a fresh reader can spot gaps that are hard to see in one's own work.

qa.q: How does Tushar see the plan to rebuild?
qa.a: Tushar sees it as smarter than sending the same file to ten more places, so the week of work looks worth it.

grounding: Illustrates asking recruiters for feedback after rejections, finding that the portfolio lacks business context, and rebuilding it.

subtype: Approach: find a mentor in the target field [Action]
passage: I'm Arnab, and I share a hostel room with Abhinav. Last week I watched Abhinav find an alumnus on the college network who works in product design. The message was four lines: who Abhinav was, which course, one specific question, and a request for a fifteen-minute call. A reply came in two days. After the call Abhinav sat at the desk with the notebook open and typed a thank-you that listed three things learned: most hiring starts with a small design test, two solid case studies beat ten screenshots, and one internship deadline is never posted anywhere public. The alumnus answered with a single line and offered an introduction to a colleague. I can't say what Abhinav was hoping for, but the room was quieter and the notebook fuller than usual.

qa.q: How long did the alumnus take to reply to the message?
qa.a: A reply came in two days.

qa.q: What do the quieter room and fuller notebook suggest about how Abhinav felt after the call?
qa.a: They suggest Abhinav felt focused and encouraged, though Arnab admits this is only a guess.

qa.q: What else could Abhinav try, and why?
qa.a: Abhinav could make one small case study and ask the alumnus to look at it, because concrete work gives a mentor something specific to comment on.

qa.q: How might the alumnus feel about receiving the thank-you summary?
qa.a: The alumnus probably felt respected and glad to help, since the summary showed the call was used well and led to an offer of an introduction.

grounding: Illustrates writing to an alumnus in the desired field, asking for a short call and following up with a summary of what was learned.

subtype: Approach: assume skills transfer without checking [Pitfall]
passage:
Day 1. Over tea, Lalit tells Vijay, "Twenty-five kids in a room and I can hold every one of them. Sales is just talking." The company's product-training video stays unwatched.

Day 9. The target sheet says forty calls a day. Lalit's first cold call ends in a click after eight seconds. So does the second. Explaining everything patiently, the way it works in a classroom, gets nowhere when the listener can simply hang up. By evening Lalit has booked no visits at all.

Day 21. Lalit is far behind on targets. Vijay says, "You never asked what the job needed." Lalit opens a notebook and writes two columns: what I assumed, and what actually happened. The second column is much longer.

qa.q: How many calls a day did the target sheet require?
qa.a: The target sheet said forty calls a day.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling after the first cold call ended in a click?
qa.a: Lalit felt surprised and rattled, because the confidence from the classroom did not work on a stranger who could hang up.

qa.q: What could Lalit have done before the first day to test the assumption?
qa.a: Lalit could have listened in on a senior's calls or practised a few mock cold calls, so the gaps showed up early instead of against targets.

qa.q: How might Vijay see Lalit's plan?
qa.a: Vijay may see it as confident but untested, and may feel concerned watching Lalit skip the training video and then fall behind.

grounding: Illustrates a teacher moving into sales who assumes classroom skills will transfer and is caught out by targets and cold-calling.

subtype: Approach: check safety and call emergency services first [Action]
passage:
Note to file, written the evening of the crash.

A scooter and a van collided at the junction outside the gate. Shalini, a second-year student walking ahead of me, stopped at once, stepped onto the pavement and looked back along the road before going near. Then Shalini raised a hand to slow a lorry, dialled 112 and said clearly: "One person on the road, awake, a van blocking the left lane, outside the college gate." I stayed beside the rider. Shalini went to the corner to wave the ambulance in. The police arrived soon after and took over.

Shalini's voice stayed steady on the call, but the hands were shaking afterwards. I've asked Shalini to come and see me tomorrow, just to talk.

Kishore, faculty coordinator

qa.q: Which number did Shalini dial?
qa.a: Shalini dialled 112.

qa.q: What do Shalini's shaking hands suggest about how Shalini felt?
qa.a: They suggest Shalini was frightened and shaken after the event, even though the voice on the call stayed steady.

qa.q: What could Shalini and Kishore do while waiting for the ambulance, and why?
qa.a: They could ask a bystander to keep other people back and stay on the line for instructions, because trained responders can guide them and crowds add risk.

qa.q: How might the rider have experienced the minutes before help came?
qa.a: The rider probably felt scared and hurt but a little safer knowing someone stayed close and help had been called.

grounding: Illustrates a young bystander first checking for traffic danger, moving to a safe spot and calling the emergency number.

subtype: Approach: stay calm and follow a simple mental checklist [Thinking]
passage:
Rain was coming down hard on the flyover road when a scooter skidded and slid across the tarmac. Binita, walking home with her classmate Omkar, felt her stomach drop. Her phone showed nine percent battery.

Safety first, she told herself, the way the first-aid instructor had put it. Are cars still coming? She pulled Omkar behind the barrier. "Hold your torch up and wave it at the traffic." Then: call for help. She dialled 112 with wet fingers. Don't move the rider unless there's danger. There was no fire, so she crouched beside the rider and kept still. Say only what you know. "A scooter has fallen near the bus stop on the flyover. One person on the ground, awake, talking. I don't know more than that."

The phone dropped to eight percent as the siren sounded.

qa.q: What was the battery percentage on Binita's phone?
qa.a: Her phone showed nine percent battery.

qa.q: What is Binita feeling as she stands over the rider in the rain?
qa.a: Binita is nervous and frightened, and she steadies herself by repeating the checklist from the first-aid class.

qa.q: What could Binita do if she couldn't remember the checklist, and why?
qa.a: She could ask the emergency operator what to do next and stick to what she can see, because the operator is trained to guide callers.

qa.q: How might the situation look to Omkar?
qa.a: Omkar probably feels unsure but relieved to be given a clear job with the torch, because Binita's calm steps give the moment some structure.

grounding: Illustrates recalling a first-aid class outline and following it in order at a crash scene under stress.

subtype: Approach: freeze and film the scene instead of helping [Pitfall]
passage:
Note to file, written the evening of the accident.

I reached the crossing from the market and found about a dozen people standing at the kerb, most with phones held up. Preeti, a first-year student, was one of them, filming. The delivery rider lay beside the kerb with one arm over the face. A shopkeeper told me it had been about six minutes and, as far as anyone knew, no call had been made; each person had assumed another had done it. I dialled 112. The ambulance arrived soon after.

Afterwards Preeti stood still with the phone still in hand and said, "I kept thinking someone else would do it." I sat with Preeti on the step and did not lecture. I asked what the video was for, and Preeti had no answer. I will invite Preeti to the next first-aid session.

Abhinav, hostel warden

qa.q: How long had the rider been on the road before anyone called for help?
qa.a: It had been about six minutes when the shopkeeper told the writer, and no call had been made.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling as the ambulance left?
qa.a: Preeti seemed stunned and regretful, standing still with the phone in hand and admitting to thinking someone else would make the call.

qa.q: What could Preeti do differently next time, and why?
qa.a: Preeti could put the phone down and dial the emergency number straight away, or point at one person and ask them to call, because when everyone assumes someone else has called, no one does.

qa.q: How might the rider have experienced those minutes?
qa.a: The rider probably felt frightened and alone on the ground while people nearby only watched and waited.

grounding: Illustrates a person freezing and filming a crash while the injured rider waits and nobody calls for help for several minutes.

passage:
Incident register, evening shift. A car braked hard at the pump entrance and knocked a cyclist down. Ten or so people stopped and stared. Vikas, a second-year student who had been filling up his scooter, pointed at a woman in a green sari: "You, phone 112 now, tell them it's the pump on Ring Road." To two men: "You two, hold the traffic back behind that car." To the boy from the tea stall: "Water, and a blanket from the office." Then Vikas crouched beside the cyclist, who was talking, and did not move the cyclist. Nobody argued. People who had been frozen a minute earlier were suddenly busy. I unlocked the office for the blanket, then noted the car's number and saved the camera footage for the police.

Karthik, supervisor, petrol pump

qa.q: Which number did Vikas tell the woman in the green sari to call?
qa.a: Vikas told the woman to phone 112.

qa.q: What does Vikas crouching beside the cyclist without moving the cyclist suggest about Vikas's thinking?
qa.a: It suggests Vikas was cautious and concerned, wanting to stay close and comfort the cyclist without risking more harm.

qa.q: What could another bystander do in a crowd like this, and why?
qa.a: Any bystander could copy this: pick one person to call 112 and give out jobs by pointing, because a specific request breaks the wait for someone else to act.

qa.q: How might the woman in the green sari have felt when Vikas pointed at her?
qa.a: She was probably startled but relieved to get a clear job, since she had been frozen with the crowd and now knew what to do.

grounding: Illustrates a young person assigning clear tasks to bystanders (call for help, stop traffic, fetch water and a blanket).

subtype: Approach: when involved, exchange details and document the scene [Action]
passage: The bump was small. Paulo's mother's hatchback had rolled into the back of a delivery van at a red light in Porto. Paulo switched off the engine, put on the hazard lights and got out. "Is everyone all right?" His friend Ines in the passenger seat nodded, and so did Gabriel, the van driver. Paulo took photos of both bumpers, the road and the van's number plate, then wrote down Gabriel's insurer and phone number. Gabriel began to argue about who had braked late. "The photos will show it," Paulo said quietly. "Let's leave that to the insurers." If either of them had been hurt or refused to share details, Paulo would have called the police. Back in the car his hands were still tight on the wheel, but he texted his mother: "Nobody hurt. Car okay. Photos taken."

qa.q: What did Paulo photograph at the scene?
qa.a: Paulo took photos of both bumpers, the road and the van's number plate.

qa.q: How was Paulo feeling after the collision, judging by his hands?
qa.a: Paulo was still tense and shaken, even though he had stayed calm on the outside.

qa.q: What could Paulo do if Gabriel refused to give an insurer's name, and why?
qa.a: Paulo could stay calm, keep the plate photo and call the police so the details are officially recorded, which protects both drivers without a quarrel.

qa.q: How might Gabriel have felt about being asked for details rather than being argued with?
qa.a: Gabriel may have felt irritated at first at not getting a quarrel, then relieved that the exchange stayed calm and clear.

grounding: Illustrates a driver in a minor collision checking everyone is unhurt, photographing the scene and swapping details calmly.

subtype: Approach: argue over blame at the roadside [Pitfall]
passage:
Wednesday, 9 pm. Still shaking. My scooter clipped a car coming out of the lane by the market, or the car cut across me. I still think that. The driver, Dolma, jumped out yelling that I was going too fast, and I yelled back. We stood in the road pointing at scratches for ages. A crowd gathered. Nobody was looking at the cyclist who had swerved around us and gone down by the wall, holding his knee. A man from the tea stall finally shouted, "He's hurt and you two are arguing!" My face burned. Dolma went quiet too. Somebody else had already called 112. I still think I was right about the turn, but I can't explain why I never checked on the cyclist first. I don't even know his name.

Kavitha

qa.q: Where did the cyclist end up after swerving?
qa.a: The cyclist went down by the wall, holding his knee.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling when the man from the tea stall shouted?
qa.a: Kavitha felt ashamed and embarrassed, since Kavitha's face burned and Kavitha realised the cyclist had never been checked on.

qa.q: What could the two drivers have done first instead of arguing, and why?
qa.a: They could have checked on the cyclist and called for help, then left the blame for the insurers or police, because the injured person's needs come first.

qa.q: How might the cyclist have experienced those minutes by the wall?
qa.a: The cyclist was probably in pain and feeling ignored while the two people who caused the swerve argued about fault.

grounding: Illustrates two drivers shouting about blame at the roadside while an injured cyclist waits and a crowd gathers.

subtype: Approach: seek support and review habits afterwards [Revision]
passage:
Dear Akash,

You asked how I am, and typing "fine" felt wrong, so here is the real answer. Two weeks ago I skidded on gravel riding home at eleven at night. My shoulder is bruised and the headaches kept coming back after dark. I finally told Mum and Dad everything on Sunday, and Dad took me to the doctor, who checked me over. I'm going back for a follow-up next week.

I have made new rules and taped them next to my helmet shelf: strap the helmet on every single ride, stay under the limit even when friends pull ahead, and no riding after nine at night. I'll take the bus instead. It feels like giving up some freedom, but it also feels like the fall taught me something. Come over and I'll tell you the whole story.

Aparna

qa.q: Which rules did Aparna tape next to the helmet shelf?
qa.a: Strap the helmet on every ride, stay under the limit, and no riding after nine at night.

qa.q: How does Aparna feel about the new rules?
qa.a: Aparna's feelings are mixed: it feels like giving up some freedom, but Aparna also feels the fall taught something useful.

qa.q: What else could Aparna do to make the new habits last, and why?
qa.a: Aparna could ask Akash or a friend to check in on the rules and keep the follow-up visit, because support makes new habits easier to keep.

qa.q: How might Aparna's parents have felt on hearing everything on Sunday?
qa.a: They were probably worried and also relieved that Aparna finally told them, since it let Dad take Aparna to the doctor.

grounding: Illustrates a shaken person talking with family, seeing a doctor and adopting stricter rules on helmets, speed and night riding.
